title: The Truth about Relativity
coreMove: Remove the planted comparison and rebuild the choice around the options that actually compete for your goal.
sourcePressure: The source centers on relativity, the Economist subscription decoy, and the way nearby comparisons make an option feel valuable without proving absolute worth.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: The weak version says comparison is bad; the precise lesson is that easy comparison can replace the real comparison set.

hook: The expensive option is not the trap

exampleSpecs.domain: museum membership desk with one deliberately weak patron tier
exampleSpecs.audience: a museum visitor choosing an annual membership before a family exhibit opens
exampleSpecs.stakes: committing to a donation level that may be steered by a decoy instead of actual visit plans
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the visitor covers the middle tier on the laminated rate sheet with a receipt and checks whether the premium tier still looks worth buying
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a laminated membership sheet clipped to a brass stand beside the coat-check counter

exampleSpecs.domain: fish market stall comparing catch boxes before dawn
exampleSpecs.audience: a restaurant buyer choosing between seafood boxes under time pressure
exampleSpecs.stakes: overpaying for the largest box because a smaller damaged box makes it look clean
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the buyer turns the cracked foam box backward so it cannot act as the loser, then reprices the remaining two boxes by portions served
exampleSpecs.firstImage: three foam seafood boxes sweating on crushed ice under a hanging scale

exampleSpecs.audience: a volunteer choosing between single-film, weekday, and all-access passes
exampleSpecs.stakes: spending a week's food budget because the all-access pass dominates a badly priced weekday pass
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the volunteer writes the films they can actually attend on the back of the program before looking at the decoy pass again
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a folded festival program with showtimes circled in pencil

exampleSpecs.domain: farm equipment rental counter during harvest week
exampleSpecs.audience: a small orchard owner comparing lift rentals
exampleSpecs.stakes: renting an oversized lift because a useless mid-size option makes it look prudent
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the owner steps outside and marks the actual branch height on the rental yard fence before choosing between lifts
exampleSpecs.firstImage: mud on the rental office mat beside a clipboard of lift heights

exampleSpecs.audience: a treasurer evaluating fabric packages for a community choir
exampleSpecs.stakes: using donor money on premium trim because the plain-but-overpriced package creates an easy contrast
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the treasurer lays the fabric swatches over the price labels and asks which one meets the choir's actual durability rule
exampleSpecs.firstImage: three fabric swatches pinned to a felt bulletin strip in a church basement office

exampleSpecs.domain: boat storage contract at a winter marina
exampleSpecs.audience: a first-time boat owner choosing storage before the first freeze
exampleSpecs.stakes: buying unnecessary indoor storage because a bad outdoor-plus-service option pushes the premium plan
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: after ignoring the weak middle contract, the owner measures actual winter access needs against the basic covered rack
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a salt-stiff contract packet flapping under a marina office paperweight

skillTargets: spot a decoy option that exists to lose
distinguish absolute fit from relative dominance
explain why confidence can rise when the frame is rigged

tryThisNowSpec: Take one active choice with three options and physically cover the option that mainly makes another option look good; decide whether the winner still solves the original need.
